Shifted primes in arithmetic progressions to large moduli with linear sieve remainder weights

Ruiyi Zhang Independent Researcher, Columbia, Maryland, USA
Abstract.

Let NN be a sufficiently large even integer, and fix B>0B>0 and 0<ε≤10−40<\varepsilon\leq 10^{-4}. Take Iwaniec’s upper or lower linear-sieve remainder weights. We estimate a signed sum of prime-counting discrepancies on N/(log⁡N)B<p<(1−ε)⁢NN/(\log N)^{B}<p<(1-\varepsilon)N. Fix 0<u≤1/5000<u\leq 1/500 and a sieve exponent 1/2<θ<(5−7/32−3⁢u)/81/2<\theta<(5-7/32-3u)/8. Choose 0<σ≤min⁡{10−10,((5−7/32−3⁢u)/8−θ)/200,u/(2⁢θ)}0<\sigma\leq\min\{10^{-10},((5-7/32-3u)/8-\theta)/200,\sqrt{u/(2\theta)}\}. Then the complete modulus support lies below N(5−7/32−3⁢u)/8N^{(5-7/32-3u)/8}. For every fixed saving exponent A>0A>0, the error is O⁢(N⁢(log⁡N)−A)O(N(\log N)^{-A}). For each of the two signs ν∈{+,−}\nu\in\{+,-\}, the result holds uniformly for integers a∈[N,N⁢log⁡N/3]a\in[N,N\log N/3] satisfying (a,q)=1(a,q)=1 for every modulus qq in the support of the corresponding coefficient wNνw_{N}^{\nu}. Call these shifts admissible; they form a subset of the interval that includes a=Na=N. When u=1/500u=1/500 and θ=19101/32000−10−4\theta=19101/32000-10^{-4}, the ratio log⁡D/log⁡z\log D/\log z is 298.403125298.403125. The proof keeps the smooth-divisor and prime-tuple factors of the linear-sieve weights. It combines dispersion with a Heath–Brown decomposition. The boundary, Type-I and Type-II terms are estimated separately.

Key words and phrases:
shifted primes, linear sieve, level of distribution, dispersion method, Kloosterman sums, primes in arithmetic progressions

1. Introduction

The Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem [2, 3] gives level 1/21/2 for primes in arithmetic progressions on average. Related early weighted work includes Fouvry–Iwaniec [19, 20]. Consider weighted sums with a fixed residue. Bombieri–Friedlander–Iwaniec reached level 4/74/7 with well-factorable weights [6, Theorem 10]. With a fixed residue, Maynard [7, Theorems 1.1–1.2] proved level 3/53/5 for triply well-factorable weights and level 7/127/12 for the upper linear-sieve weights. Parts I–III address fixed residue classes, well-factorable estimates, and uniform residue classes, respectively [21, 7, 22]. Lichtman [1, Theorem 1.7, (1.6)] obtained level 66/10766/107 for triply well-factorable weights with a fixed residue. For such weights he also obtained level 153/256−δ153/256-\delta, uniformly over residues |a|<N1+δ|a|<N^{1+\delta} for each fixed δ>0\delta>0 [1, Theorem 1.7, (1.7)]. His Proposition 6.6 treats Iwaniec’s modified upper and lower linear-sieve weights. There the largest prime factors are restricted to prescribed short intervals. Its admissible level is ϑ≤ϑ⁢(t1)−δ\vartheta\leq\boldsymbol{\vartheta}(t_{1})-\delta with ϑ⁢(t1)\boldsymbol{\vartheta}(t_{1}) defined in [1, (6.2)]. Take at least three prescribed factors and t1t_{1} below the threshold in that proposition. Then the level becomes ϑ≤ϑ⁢(t1,t2,t3)−δ\vartheta\leq\boldsymbol{\vartheta}(t_{1},t_{2},t_{3})-\delta, with the function of [1, (6.4)] and fixed δ>0\delta>0. The error constant in that proposition depends on the fixed residue aa [1, Proposition 6.6]. Lichtman’s modified linear-sieve weights reach level 10/1710/17 [25].

Pascadi [8, Theorem 1.3] gives levels approaching 5/85/8 for triply well-factorable weights, with a fixed residue. For suitable upper linear-sieve weights his levels approach 3/53/5. Pascadi’s Theorem 5.4 also treats both signs of the restricted well-factorable linear-sieve weights and refines Proposition 6.6 [8, Theorem 5.4]. His Lemma 5.6 records a correction to a small error in Section 6 of [1] [8, Lemma 5.6].

Here z=Nuz=N^{u} with u≤1/500u\leq 1/500 and θ>1/2\theta>1/2, so s=θ/u>250s=\theta/u>250, in the fundamental-lemma range. The cited linear-sieve levels use sifting ranges with s≈1s\approx 1–22 and are not directly comparable.

The congruence p≡a(modq)p\equiv a\pmod{q} says that qq divides the shifted prime a−pa-p. So the sums below count shifted primes a−pa-p in the class 0 modulo qq. The modulus coefficients are Iwaniec’s explicit lower and upper remainder weights [10, Theorem 4]. We retain their smooth-divisor factors, prime-tuple factors, and distinctness conditions. We estimate the complete signed sum for the admissible shifts in the stated interval. Theorem 1.2 covers the fixed parameters u,θ,A,B,εu,\theta,A,B,\varepsilon below. Its support exponent tends to 153/256153/256 as u↓0u\downarrow 0. This numerical endpoint matches Lichtman’s moving-residue level for triply well-factorable weights [1, Theorem 1.7, (1.7)]; the residue ranges differ. At u=1/500u=1/500 the exponent is smaller. The coefficient family here is the full remainder in [10, Theorem 4]. It includes the smooth-only term and the distinctness masks. Lichtman’s Proposition 6.6 estimates restricted factor-pattern components of different modified sieve weights. Its implied constant depends on the fixed residue. Here uniformity is only over the support-coprime shifts specified below, an admissible subset of [N,N⁢log⁡N/3][N,N\log N/3] that includes a=Na=N; no uniformity over the full interval is asserted.

Proof of Theorem 1.1.

Apply Theorem 1.2 with u=1/500u=1/500. Then Θ⁢(u)=19101/32000\Theta(u)=19101/32000, and its condition on σ\sigma becomes the displayed condition above. All the support, coefficient, and discrepancy bounds specialize as stated. The numerical sieve ratio follows from log⁡D/log⁡z=θ/u\log D/\log z=\theta/u. At θ=19101/32000−10−4\theta=19101/32000-10^{-4} the proof uses Theorem 3.2 through Theorem 1.2. That theorem allows support up to X0.6X^{0.6}. It does not use the introductory proposition. The introductory source-box estimate has the fixed local level ϑ0=19101/32000−10−4\vartheta_{0}=19101/32000-10^{-4}. It assumes its support hypothesis. The packing ceiling for Theorem 1.2 is Θ⁢(u)\Theta(u). The latter applies the X0.6X^{0.6} dispersion theorem 3.2 together with the source estimates below. Here Θ⁢(u)<153/256<0.6\Theta(u)<153/256<0.6. Thus the full support of Iwaniec’s remainder weights lies in the range of Theorem 3.2. Section 4 proves the modulus packing. Appendix B estimates the Heath–Brown, boundary, and other source terms. Section 5 assembles these estimates.

The proof uses the spectral large sieves of Deshouillers and Iwaniec [5]. It uses the Kim–Sarnak exponent 7/647/64 [13]. It also uses Deligne’s bound for holomorphic coefficients [14]. Section 2 states these inputs. The dispersion argument and its application are in Sections 3–5.

2.1. Spectral normalization and large sieves

The spectral large sieves are due to Deshouillers and Iwaniec [5].

3. Dispersion for abstract sources

This section proves a local implication for an abstract source. It uses Linnik’s dispersion method [28]. The second-dispersion setup has close precedents in Maynard [7] and Lichtman [1, §5]; the proof below tracks its own coefficient masks, restoration terms, and moving residue. The local hypotheses are (H1)–(H5). The source-wide estimate (H6) and the box-family coefficient bound (H7) are used only in the global summation in Section 3.10. Each application verifies the required conditions for its own measures. The geometric and source partition results appear below. Theorem 2.8 is stated in Section 2, (2.38)–(2.43), and derived from the classical inputs in §2.7. We keep its full moving-frequency bracket. The local estimate has three terms. The restoration error EGRE_{\rm GR} is bounded apart from the spectral term.

4. Three-slot packing for Iwaniec’s remainder coefficients

This section proves a general packing theorem. It then verifies the hypotheses for the remainder coefficients of Iwaniec’s linear sieve [10, Theorem 4]. The packing and coefficient identities provide the modulus factorization used in the prime-discrepancy estimates below. The functions below specialize Lichtman’s optimization [1, Proposition 6.1, (6.2), (6.4)] to spectral exponent 7/327/32 and moving-residue exponent 11. We prove the labelled-atom statement here; its two-bin step is related to the corrected argument in Pascadi’s Lemma 5.6 [8].

for every fixed A>0A>0. Strict endpoint conventions contribute at most two primes. Multiply this error by the reciprocal-totient sum and apply (1.2). ∎

The source input used for the coefficients in formula (W) is [10, Theorem 4]. Its hypotheses are [10, (1)–(2)]. Its upper inequality permits 2≤z≤D2\leq z\leq D; its lower inequality permits 2≤z≤D1/22\leq z\leq D^{1/2}. Fix 0<u≤1/5000<u\leq 1/500 and 1/2<θ<Θ⁢(u)1/2<\theta<\Theta(u) as in Theorem 1.2. Then D=NθD=N^{\theta} and z=Nuz=N^{u} satisfy 2⁢u<θ2u<\theta. Thus both ranges apply for all sufficiently large NN. The choice σ≤u/(2⁢θ)\sigma\leq\sqrt{u/(2\theta)} also gives Y=Dσ2≤Nu/2<zY=D^{\sigma^{2}}\leq N^{u/2}<z. The mesh is ϵs=σ\epsilon_{s}=\sigma and δs=σ9=τ\delta_{s}=\sigma^{9}=\tau. The smooth-prime cutoff is YY, as in (2.28)–(2.33b).

Theorem 4’s printed argument list of λdν\lambda_{d}^{\nu} contains the mesh parameter and box tuple. It contains neither the sequence nor the cutoff. The construction in [10, (23)–(26)] collects universal Rosser and fundamental-lemma coefficients. The sequence enters through r⁢(𝒜,q)r(\mathcal{A},q). At each cutoff zz, we use the coefficients and prime-tuple support supplied by that construction. The coefficient family is independent of the sequence. It may depend on zz. The signed prime-source estimate is proved separately in Appendix B.

The OO-constant in the main-term error of [10, Theorem 4] is not given numerically.

The proof of Theorem 1.2 uses no finite computation.

A box is Type II if some ei∈𝒲e_{i}\in\mathcal{W}. Select the largest such eie_{i}, with ties broken by the fixed variable order. Suppose no exponent lies in 𝒲\mathcal{W}. A box is Type I-1 when it has exactly one large variable and that variable is not a Möbius variable. It is Type I-2 when it has exactly two large variables and neither is a Möbius variable. There are no other nonboundary boxes. In fact, a large Möbius variable would imply 14⁢σ≤κX−ωX/3≤σ/20214\sigma\leq\kappa_{X}-\omega_{X}/3\leq\sigma/202. The packing lemmas give, for each Iwaniec vector, the exact three-slot coefficient and the packing inequalities (3.6)–(3.7). They include the empty-tail term and retain repeated-prime multiplicity before the mask error (B.6). The selected rough unit, Möbius and normalized-log coefficients are the three classes in (3.8). Proposition B.4 (Iwaniec prime-source estimate).

Take the parameters of Theorem 1.2, either Iwaniec sign ν\nu, and a sufficiently large even NN. Let wNνw_{N}^{\nu} be the exact coefficient (W). Let aa satisfy the residue conditions of Theorem 1.2, and let ΔD\Delta_{D} be (B.1). First split off the LOG correction algebraically. Then every remaining source summand is assigned exactly once to one class. The classes are mask, proper-power, boundary, Type-II, Type-I-1 and Type-I-2. Every retained box has the scale and coefficient properties stated above, and

(B.32) |∑qwNν⁢(q)⁢ΔD⁢(q;a)|≪σ,A,u,θ,B,ε,CboxN⁢L−A.\left|\sum_{q}w_{N}^{\nu}(q)\Delta_{D}(q;a)\right|\ll_{\sigma,A,u,\theta,B,% \varepsilon,C_{\rm box}}NL^{-A}.

Proof. The Iwaniec mask partition and support are (B.2)–(B.6). The explicit identities (B.7)–(B.11) partition the remaining tested measure into proper powers and HB tuples. The equal-ratio mesh puts each tuple in exactly one box. A face-straddling box belongs to the boundary class. On every other box both source predicates are constant. The exponent-polytope argument above puts every nonempty such box in exactly one of II, I-1 and I-2. The displayed tie rule selects one II factor. LOG is split off algebraically before that assignment. The errors are (B.6), (B.8), (B.18), (B.19) and (B.31). Their sum is Oσ,A,u,θ,B,ε,Cbox⁢(N⁢L−A)O_{\sigma,A,u,\theta,B,\varepsilon,C_{\rm box}}(NL^{-A}). □\square
